{"id": "41a50df9-f1b9-4e68-9f63-391e5b9b87c8", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_LlOzyPCuCBXWMSVlSXBjpm", "content": [{"text": "     1	---
     2	name: storage-ebs-expertise
     3	description: >
     4	  Use this skill when a user wants to know why Amazon EBS storage is slow, why an
     5	  EBS alarm fired, or whether their EBS setup is production-ready, even if they only
     6	  say an app or database on EC2 got slower or ask whether to add IOPS. Use it for
     7	  alarms on AWS/EBS metrics (VolumeReadOps, VolumeWriteOps, VolumeReadBytes,
     8	  VolumeWriteBytes, VolumeQueueLength, VolumeTotalReadTime/WriteTime,
     9	  VolumeAvgReadLatency, BurstBalance) or EBSIOBalance%/EBSByteBalance%; for sizing
     10	  IOPS or throughput changes; for a volume modification that looks stuck or failed;
     11	  for deciding which snapshots or AMIs are safe to delete or how to recover them;
     12	  for KMS errors on encrypted volumes; for EBS quota or limit errors; for a jump in
     13	  the EBS bill; and for a pre-launch EBS review. Do not use it for S3, EFS, FSx,
     14	  instance store, or EC2 problems unrelated to EBS.
     15	metadata:
     16	  author: dewavic
     17	  version: "1.0.0"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS KMS, AWS CloudTrail, Service Quotas"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     21	---
     22	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     23	
     24	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     25	
     26	## When to Use This Skill
     27	
     28	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     29	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     30	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     31	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots are safe to delete.
     32	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     33	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     34	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     35	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     36	
     37	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     38	
     39	## Prerequisites
     40	
     41	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     42	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     43	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     44	
     45	---
     46	
     47	## Workflow
     48	
     49	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     50	
     51	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     52	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     53	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     54	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     55	
     56	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     57	
     58	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     59	|---|---|---|
     60	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     61	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     62	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     63	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     64	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     65	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     66	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     67	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     68	
     69	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     70	
     71	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     72	
     73	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     74	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     75	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     76	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     77	
     78	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     79	
     80	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     81	
     82	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     83	
     84	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     85	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     86	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, or Not applicable.
     87	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     88	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     89	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     90	
     91	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every review answer starts with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`.
     92	
     93	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     94	
     95	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     96	
     97	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     98	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom.
     99	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     100	- Every "safe to delete" verdict is backed by the checks its tier requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not safe to delete.
     101	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     102	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     103	
     104	---
     105	
     106	## Critical Rules
     107	
     108	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, DeleteSnapshot, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     109	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     110	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     111	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     112	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     113	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     114	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     115	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. AWS CloudTrail is optional; `DescribeVolumesModifications` is the change record.
     116	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     117	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     118	
     119	## Error Handling
     120	
     121	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     122	
     123	## References
     124	
     125	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     126	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): safe-to-delete tiers, copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     127	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     128	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     129	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     130	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     131	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     132	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     133	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     134	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     135	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "ec3d7e82-3e9a-490a-95f2-0e9477c29f71", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_cklj79ITjryOR4MhOcaUGF", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history (when it first entered ALARM).
     17	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     18	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     19	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     20	
     21	### Step 2: Build the context
     22	
     23	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     24	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     25	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     26	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     27	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.
     28	
     29	### Step 2b: Rule EBS in or out (chat requests with no EBS alarm only)
     30	
     31	This check runs only when the run did not start from an AWS/EBS alarm or an `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` alarm, for example a chat request such as "my app is slow, is it storage?". When an EBS alarm triggered the run, skip this step and run Steps 3 to 6 in full.
     32	
     33	Read `CPUUtilization` for the instance, and the latency, `VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance` (gp2, st1, sc1) and instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` (if published) for the volumes found in Step 2, over the same window. Use the qualitative attribution matrix in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). Report "Not EBS" and stop tuning storage only if all of these hold: CPU is high, volume latency and queue length are normal, no `DescribeVolumeStatus` problem was found, and no burst or instance balance is draining or at 0. Otherwise continue with Step 3.
     34	
     35	### Step 3: Measure each volume on the dimension(s) its type is limited by
     36	
     37	Pull the last 30 minutes of AWS/EBS metrics at 1-minute granularity.
     38	
     39	- Actual IOPS = (VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds
     40	- Actual throughput = (VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period, in MiB/s
     41	- Avg latency = VolumeTotalRead/WriteTime / ops; VolumeQueueLength
     42	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both dimensions, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 for MiB/s. `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only. If `VolumeAvg*` returns nothing, use the Sum-based math above.
     43	- Always read `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds in the period with no read or write submitted; `VolumeId` only). Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period seconds x 100. Report it as evidence for every volume. Near 0 means I/O was submitted for the whole period, which fits both saturation and impairment, so use Step 5 to tell them apart. A volume that is mostly idle during the alarm window is unlikely to be the binding volume. There is no fixed band; compare with the volume's own history.
     44	
     45	Apply the rule for the volume's type:
     46	
     47	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     48	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     49	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops. Throughput is derived from IOPS x I/O size, not provisioned separately. Do NOT use VolumeThroughputPercentage to judge throughput on io1/io2; it reports the % of provisioned IOPS delivered.
     50	- st1/sc1: throughput-oriented with burst credits; compare MiB/s to the baseline/burst for the size and check BurstBalance.
     51	- Judge io2 by IOPS; judge gp3 by throughput and IOPS. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     52	
     53	### Step 4: Check the instance layer
     54	
     55	- Sum actual IOPS and MiB/s across all attached volumes; compare to the instance type's EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes.
     56	- Aggregate across ALL attached volumes, including the root volume.
     57	- Check EBSIOBalance% / EBSByteBalance%. If they are draining or at 0, or the sum is at the instance limit, the INSTANCE is the binding layer and raising volume provisioning will not help.
     58	- If instance metrics are healthy and a volume is at its own limit, the VOLUME is the binding layer.
     59	- If `EBSIOBalance%` is absent, the instance size does not publish it. Use the summed values against the baseline.
     60	
     61	### Step 5: Distinguish saturation from impairment
     62	
     63	If queue length and latency are elevated but the volume and instance are both below their limits, this is NOT saturation. Suspect an impairment or injected latency; do NOT recommend increasing provisioning.
     64	
     65	The impairment signature is IOPS and throughput collapsing while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Saturation looks different: metrics flat at the provisioned limit with modest latency. When you see the impairment signature, check in this order:
     66	
     67	1. The `DescribeVolumeStatus` result from Step 2 (impaired status, failing checks, scheduled events). Read it again if the symptom started after Step 2.
     68	2. AWS Health `DescribeEvents` for Amazon EBS and Amazon EC2 events in the Region and Availability Zone.
     69	3. AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment that targets the volume or instance, with actions `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io`. If one is running, say so plainly: the latency is injected and will end with the experiment.
     70	
     71	If none explains it, follow the escalation rules in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md).
     72	
     73	### Step 5b: Recent changes (optional)
     74	
     75	Read `DescribeVolumesModifications` for every attached volume first. It is the authoritative change record. An AWS CloudTrail `LookupEvents` search for `ModifyVolume`, `AttachVolume`, `DetachVolume` and `ModifyInstanceAttribute` is optional and only if available. If it is denied or empty, note it under Gaps and continue.
     76	
     77	### Step 6: Report
     78	
     79	For each affected volume: type, provisioned vs actual, the binding dimension, and whether the volume or the instance is the binding layer. Recommend specific Elastic Volumes changes with target values (raise IOPS, raise gp3 throughput, change type, e.g. gp2 -> gp3), or an instance type change if the instance is the limit. Use MiB/s for throughput.
     80	
     81	Write the report with the verdict template in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) (Answer, Evidence, Binding layer, Recommendation, Separate findings, Gaps).
     82	
     83	Elastic Volumes rules: up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window; each must finish (modifying -> optimizing -> completed) before the next can start. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change). Rollback is possible once the modification completes, within that limit.
     84	
     85	Sizing rules for any recommended target:
     86	
     87	- Keep the SUM of all volumes attached to the instance within the instance's EBS BASELINE (DescribeInstanceTypes), not its burst maximum. If the target would exceed it, say so and lower the target, or recommend an instance type change.
     88	- gp3 throughput must not exceed 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS.
     89	- State how the target was computed (measured demand, type rule, instance baseline minus other volumes' usage).
     90	
     91	## Other performance topics
     92	
     93	### Micro-bursting
     94	
     95	AWS/EBS data is 1-minute. Sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average stays below it. If latency or queue length rises while the average is below the limit, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. Do not claim headroom from the average alone.
     96	
     97	### Volume initialization after restore
     98	
     99	A volume created from a snapshot loads blocks from Amazon S3 the first time they are read, which adds latency until the volume is initialized. Check `DescribeVolumes` `SnapshotId` and `CreateTime`. If the volume was recently restored, explain initialization and point to fast snapshot restore (`DescribeFastSnapshotRestores`) and the initialization guide. This is not a provisioning problem.
     100	
     101	### Burst credits
     102	
     103	- Volume level: gp2, st1 and sc1 publish `BurstBalance`. Draining or at 0 means the volume has dropped or will drop to its baseline. Recommend gp2 to gp3 migration, or a size or type that gives the needed baseline.
     104	- Instance level: some smaller instance sizes publish `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`. Draining or at 0 means the instance has dropped or will drop to its EBS baseline. Recommend an instance type whose baseline covers the measured demand.
     105	
     106	### How much IOPS or throughput to provision
     107	
     108	1. Measure peak demand per volume over a representative window (IOPS and MiB/s, Step 3 math).

     110	3. Check the instance's remaining EBS baseline: baseline minus the measured usage of the other attached volumes.
     111	4. Propose the smaller of the measured need and what the instance can deliver. If the need exceeds the instance baseline, say so and recommend an instance type change.
     112	5. State how the target was computed.

     114	## Decision rules
     115	
     116	Use the binding-layer decision tree in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). The signatures are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).

     119	
     120	The verdict template in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). When the instance is the ceiling, the Answer says: "The volume has headroom; raising volume IOPS will not help; change the instance type." Never call a volume "saturated" when it is below its own limit.

     124	- This path is read-only. Any `ModifyVolume` or instance type change is a proposal with exact parameters, expected effect, cost direction and rollback. It runs only through a directed action approved on the approval card.

     3	Use this file for any judgement about whether a volume or an instance is at a limit. Read the provisioned values from the APIs (`DescribeVolumes`, `DescribeInstanceTypes`). The numbers below are the documented service limits, not targets. Throughput is always in MiB/s.
     4	
     5	## Which dimension binds, by volume type
     6	
     7	| Type | Included or baseline | Maximum per volume | Ratio rules | Burst model | How to judge |
     8	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
     9	| gp3 | 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s included at any size | 80,000 IOPS; 2,000 MiB/s | Up to 500 IOPS per GiB; up to 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS | No burst | Compare actual IOPS to `Iops` AND actual MiB/s to `Throughput`. Either can bind. For a sequential workload, check throughput first |
     10	| gp2 | 3 IOPS per GiB, minimum 100 | 16,000 IOPS (reached at 5,334 GiB) | Size sets performance | Bursts to 3,000 IOPS while `BurstBalance` is above 0 | Compare actual IOPS to the baseline for the size. Check `BurstBalance` draining or at 0 |
     11	| io1 / io2 | Provisioned `Iops` | io2 Block Express: up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s on supported Nitro instances | io2: up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB | No burst | Judge by IOPS only. Throughput is derived from IOPS x I/O size and is not provisioned separately |
     12	| st1 | 40 MiB/s per TiB baseline | 500 MiB/s | Burst 250 MiB/s per TiB | `BurstBalance` | Compare MiB/s to the baseline and burst for the size; check `BurstBalance` |
     13	| sc1 | 12 MiB/s per TiB baseline | 250 MiB/s | Burst 80 MiB/s per TiB | `BurstBalance` | Compare MiB/s to the baseline and burst for the size; check `BurstBalance` |
     14	
     15	For io1 limits and for io2 on instances that are not supported for Block Express, read the provisioned IOPS page in Sources. Do not quote a maximum from memory.
     16	
     17	## Metric rules that change the verdict
     18	
     19	- `VolumeThroughputPercentage` exists only for Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes. It reports the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered, not MiB/s. Never use it as a throughput signal on io1 or io2. A healthy io2 volume can read 100% while its MiB/s is low.
     20	- Judge io2 by IOPS. Judge gp3 by throughput and IOPS.
     21	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both the `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` dimensions and exist only for Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 to get MiB/s.
     22	- `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only.
     23	- A 1-minute average hides sub-minute peaks. If the minute average is below a limit but latency and queue length rise, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven.

     26	
     27	| Type | Documented expectation |
     28	|---|---|
     29	| gp3 | Single-digit millisecond latency |
     30	| io2 Block Express | Under 500 microseconds average latency for 16 KiB I/O |
     31	
     32	For other types the public documentation does not give a latency number. Compare the volume against its own history in the same window on a normal day and against the type's documented expectation above.

     43	| Instance saturation | Sum across all attached volumes flat at the instance EBS baseline, or `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` draining or at 0. Each volume below its own limit | The instance is the binding layer | Change the instance type. Raising volume provisioning will not help |

     2	
     3	Load this file on every request. Every value in a verdict or a review comes from one of these calls. Tags are used for naming only, never as the source of a configuration value.
     4	
     5	## Read-only API allowlist
     6	
     7	| Service | APIs |
     8	|---|---|
     9	| Amazon EC2 | `DescribeVolumes`, `DescribeVolumeStatus`, `DescribeVolumesModifications`, `DescribeVolumeAttribute`, `DescribeInstances`, `DescribeInstanceTypes`, `DescribeInstanceAttribute`, `DescribeSnapshots`, `DescribeSnapshotAttribute`, `DescribeImages`, `DescribeFastSnapshotRestores`, `GetEbsEncryptionByDefault`, `GetEbsDefaultKmsKeyId`, `GetSnapshotBlockPublicAccessState`, `DescribeLockedSnapshots` |
     10	| Amazon CloudWatch | `DescribeAlarms`, `DescribeAlarmHistory`, `GetMetricData`, `ListMetrics` |
     11	| Service Quotas | `ListServiceQuotas`, `GetServiceQuota`, `GetAWSDefaultServiceQuota`, `ListRequestedServiceQuotaChangeHistoryByQuota` |
     12	| Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager | `GetLifecyclePolicies`, `GetLifecyclePolicy` |
     13	| Recycle Bin | `ListRules`, `GetRule` |
     14	| AWS Backup | `ListBackupPlans`, `ListBackupSelections`, `GetBackupSelection`, `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` (always with `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true; without it the call also returns snapshots AWS Backup did not create), `ListProtectedResources` |
     15	| AWS KMS | `DescribeKey`, `GetKeyPolicy`, `ListGrants` |
     16	| AWS Cost Explorer | `GetCostAndUsage`, `GetDimensionValues` |
     17	| AWS FIS | `ListExperiments`, `GetExperiment` |
     18	| AWS Health | `DescribeEvents` |
     19	| AWS Compute Optimizer (optional) | `GetEBSVolumeRecommendations` |
     20	| AWS CloudTrail (optional) | `LookupEvents`. This call is optional. If it is denied or returns nothing, record a Gap and continue. Never make it a required step |
     21	
     22	Nothing outside this list is called by the skill on its own. Mutating calls are proposals (see SKILL.md Critical rules).
     23	
     24	## Metric rules
     25	
     26	AWS/EBS publishes 1-minute data.
     27	
     28	| Namespace | Metrics | Dimensions |
     29	|---|---|---|
     30	| AWS/EBS | `VolumeAvgIOPS` (Ops/s), `VolumeAvgThroughput` (KiB/s), `VolumeAvgReadLatency`, `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` | `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`. Nitro instances only |
     31	| AWS/EBS | `VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeIdleTime`, `BurstBalance`, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` (Provisioned IOPS SSD only) | `VolumeId` |
     32	| AWS/EC2 | `EBSIOBalance%`, `EBSByteBalance%`, `EBSReadOps`, `EBSWriteOps`, `EBSReadBytes`, `EBSWriteBytes` | `InstanceId` |
     33	
     34	Metric math from the Amazon CloudWatch metrics page for Amazon EBS. Use `Sum` statistics for ops, bytes and time.
     35	
     36	- IOPS = Sum(`VolumeReadOps` + `VolumeWriteOps`) / period in seconds
     37	- MiB/s = Sum(`VolumeReadBytes` + `VolumeWriteBytes`) / period in seconds / 1,048,576
     38	- Average latency per operation = `VolumeTotalReadTime` / `VolumeReadOps` (and the write equivalent)
     39	- Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period in seconds x 100
     40	- MiB/s from `VolumeAvgThroughput` = value in KiB/s / 1,024
     41	
     42	What a 1-minute average hides: sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average looks below it (micro-bursting). When latency or queue length rises while the average sits below the limit, say that headroom is not proven instead of claiming it.
     43	
     44	`EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%` are published only for some instance sizes (generally 4xlarge and smaller) that can burst. If they are absent, the instance does not publish them. That is not a fault.

     49	|---|---|---|

     51	| A read call is held behind an operator-approval gate (for example `dlm:GetLifecyclePolicies` or `rbin:ListRules`) | The Agent Space treats it as an action | Report it as a Gap and say which conclusion stays unconfirmed. Never ask the operator to bypass the gate |

     2	
     3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.
     6	
     7	1. **Answer.** The question the user asked, answered first in one or two sentences. For example "Not stuck. The modification is in `optimizing`, which already applies the new IOPS."
     8	2. **Evidence.** The values that support the answer, each with units and the time window (for example "average `<value>` IOPS, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC"). Throughput in MiB/s.
     9	3. **Binding layer.** One of: Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, Not applicable.
     10	4. **Recommendation.** Exact parameters (volume ID, dimension, target value, how the target was computed), or "No change". Mutating steps are proposals for a directed action.
     11	5. **Separate findings.** Other true facts, labelled so they never change the Answer. For example a modification that succeeded on a volume whose instance caps delivered IOPS: the cap goes here, never as "the modification failed".
     12	6. **Gaps.** What could not be checked and why (API denied, approval gate, metric absent).
     13	
     14	## Binding-layer decision tree
     15	
     16	Work through it in order. Use measured values and the limits read from the APIs. Do not use fixed percentage triggers.
     17	
     18	1. Is the summed IOPS or MiB/s of all attached volumes flat at the instance EBS baseline, or are `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` draining or at 0?
     19	   - Yes: **Instance**. Say "the volume has headroom; raising volume IOPS will not help; change the instance type". If a volume is also flat at its own limit, report both and fix the instance first, because volume changes cannot deliver above the instance ceiling.
     20	2. Is the instance healthy and one volume flat at its own provisioned limit on the dimension its type is judged by?
     21	   - Yes: **Volume**.
     22	3. Is a gp2, st1 or sc1 volume's `BurstBalance` draining or at 0?
     23	   - Yes: **Burst credits**.
     24	4. Did an operation fail on a quota (error text names a limit)?
     25	   - Yes: **Quota**. Use the Capacity and quota headroom section of [review-operational.md](review-operational.md).
     26	5. Are all layers below their limits, latency at the volume's normal level, and queue length low?
     27	   - Yes: **Not EBS**. Check CPU, memory, network and the application.
     28	6. Are all layers below their limits but latency and `VolumeQueueLength` up while IOPS and throughput collapse?
     29	   - Yes: **AWS-side impairment** (or injected latency). Never recommend more provisioning. Follow the escalation rules below.
     30	
     31	### Qualitative attribution matrix for "is it storage?"
     32	
     33	From the attribution draft, with the numeric CPU bands removed because no public source states them.
     34	
     35	| CPU | Volume latency | Queue length | Likely attribution |
     36	|---|---|---|---|
     37	| High | High | High | Application drives heavy I/O. Both compute and storage are stressed |
     38	| High | Normal | Low | Compute, not storage |
     39	| Low | High | High | Storage. The application waits on I/O. Go to the decision tree |
     40	| Low | Normal | Low | Neither. Check network, locks and the application |
     41	
     42	"High" and "normal" mean compared with the same resource's own history and the type's documented expectation in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     43	
     44	## Escalation (shared capability)
     45	
     46	Escalate to AWS Support when either is true:
     47	
     48	- Scope signals: an open AWS Health event for the volume, Availability Zone or Region; several resources failing the same way; `DescribeVolumeStatus` reports the volume as impaired or a failing status check.
     49	- A bounded investigation cannot explain the symptom: all layers below limits, no running AWS FIS experiment, no recent change, and the symptom persists.
     50	
     51	Specific cases:
     52	
     53	- Attach or detach stuck: the attachment stays in `attaching` or `detaching` and does not progress. Diagnose (instance state, device name, whether the volume is still mounted, any forced detach already tried), then escalate. A backend action can be needed.
     54	- Modification in `optimizing` with `Progress` not increasing across several reads, or still optimizing after 24 hours. Tell the user the Amazon EBS User Guide says some performance changes take more than 24 hours, so this is a check, not a fault finding. Escalate with the evidence.
     55	- Snapshot stuck in `pending` with no progress change over the same kind of window.
     56	
     57	Evidence pack to include:
     58	
     59	1. Account placeholder, Region, volume IDs, instance IDs, snapshot IDs as read from the APIs
     60	2. The time window (first ALARM time, symptom start)
     61	3. Metric evidence with units (IOPS, MiB/s, latency, queue length, `EBSIOBalance%`, `BurstBalance`)
     62	4. Volume status and AWS Health results
     63	5. `DescribeVolumesModifications` records, and AWS CloudTrail results if that optional lookup was available
     64	6. What was ruled out and how
     65	7. The Gaps list
     66	
     67	## Review ratings
     68	
     69	Each review finding has:
     70	
     71	| Field | Values |
     72	|---|---|
     73	| Severity | `High`, `Medium`, `Low`, or `Indeterminate` (the data could not be read) |
     74	| Evidence | The values and API that show it |
     75	| Fix | A specific change with parameters |
     76	| Mutating? | Yes or No. Yes means the fix is a proposal for a directed action |
     77	
     78	Rate by impact if the risk happens, not by count. Severity guidance per area is in [review-operational.md](review-operational.md). The report layout is in [review-report-format.md](review-report-format.md).

     83	- Detaching volumes: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-detaching-volume.html

During the alarm it delivered about 1.4% of its 3,000 IOPS and about 0.5% of its 125 MiB/s, then recovered by itself when the experiment ended.

**Which volume I analysed:** the IDs in your request (`vol-0123456789abcdef0`, `i-0123456789abcdef0_1`) were rejected as invalid in account 012345678901_1. The only gp3 queue-length alarm there with a matching FIS latency experiment is `ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length`. It watches `vol-0123456789abcdef0_2` (gp3, 20 GiB, 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s), attached to `i-0123456789abcdef0_3` (c6i.xlarge). Everything below is about that volume.

**Root cause:** FIS experiment `EXP7SDntcG3Ff1fsx` (template `EXTfpFLs9urWUme`) ran `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` on this volume from 15:30:14 to 15:45:15 UTC on 2026-11-11. It added 500 ms to every write and to half the reads. The alarm was in ALARM from 15:33:08 to 15:47:08 UTC, inside that window plus normal alarm delay.

**Evidence (1-minute data, before → during the experiment):**

| Metric | Before (15:29) | During (15:31–15:44) | After (15:46+) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Write latency | 0.95 ms | 503.3 ms | 0.95 ms |
| Read latency | 0.59 ms | about 230–261 ms (500 ms on half the reads) | 0.59 ms |
| Queue length | 0.77 | 16.0, flat | back to normal |
| IOPS | 1,000 | about 42 | back to normal |
| Throughput | 15.6 MiB/s | about 0.66 MiB/s | back to normal |

- The volume was never idle during the experiment (idle time 0%).
- The workload kept about 16 I/Os in flight. At about 0.4 s each, that works out to about 42 IOPS. The added latency capped IOPS, so the provisioned limit was never in play and more IOPS would have changed nothing.

**What I ruled out:**
- **Instance limits:** the I/O and throughput burst balances stayed at 99% or higher. The instance's total EBS load during the experiment was about 43 IOPS and 0.67 MiB/s, far below its 6,000 IOPS / 149 MiB/s baseline. CPU was 0.3–1.1%.
- **Volume health and AWS-side problems:** the volume status check is ok (I/O enabled), AWS Health shows no EBS or EC2 events in us-east-1, and the volume has never been modified.
- **The current AWS outage in ap-northeast-1:** it's a different Region, and it started at 15:40:33, ten minutes after this began.

**Recommendation:** leave provisioning as it is. Things worth doing going forward:
- **Add a stop condition to the FIS template.** It has none right now.
- **Pause or annotate this alarm during planned experiments.**
- **Expect the alarm to fire again with this template.** An earlier 5-minute run (`EXP4Xs8yABzn38YDgv`, 01:07–01:12 UTC) caused the earlier alarm at 01:11–01:15 UTC.

**Other findings (they don't change the answer):**
- From 15:46 to 15:51 UTC, after the experiment, the volume ran at its full 3,000 IOPS (46.9 MiB/s) with latency under 1 ms. It was probably clearing the I/O backlog. Only if your workload regularly needs that much should you size IOPS from a representative time window; this alarm isn't a reason to.
- The instance is currently stopped.

**What I couldn't check:**
- CloudTrail wasn't queried, so I haven't confirmed who started the experiment.
- Instance-level EBS metrics are only available at 5-minute granularity.
- I didn't pull metrics for the other four attached volumes one by one; I used the instance's total instead.

## Results
**The answer to "Should we add more IOPS?" is no.** The alarm on `vol-0123456789abcdef0_2` fired because a planned AWS FIS experiment deliberately added 500 ms of latency to the volume's I/O. The volume never ran out of capacity: during the run it handled about 42 IOPS, which is 1.4% of the 3,000 provisioned. Adding IOPS would have changed nothing. The incident has already recovered on its own. The weak spot still open is that the experiment template has no stop condition, so the plan below adds one.

I proposed this plan but did not run it. It passed the safe-deployment policy check with no violations.

## Mitigation summary

**Action:** Add a CloudWatch-alarm stop condition to FIS experiment template `EXTfpFLs9urWUme`. Don't change the volume's IOPS or throughput, and keep the existing alarm as it is.

**Reasoning:**
- **What I read today (account `012345678901_1`, us-east-1):**
  - The template still has `stopConditions: [{"source": "none"}]`. It runs `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` against `[redacted ARN]` for PT15M, using role `ebs-skill-eval-fis`.
  - Both runs from this template (`EXP7SDntcG3Ff1fsx` and `EXP4Xs8yABzn38YDgv`) are `completed`.
  - The volume is unchanged: gp3, 20 GiB, 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, `in-use` on `i-0123456789abcdef0_3` as `/dev/sdh`.
- **Why a stop condition:** right now nothing stops an injection if it hurts more than intended. A run could take longer, be pointed at the wrong volume, or hit a production workload, and it would still run its full 15 minutes.
- **Why a separate guardrail alarm, not the existing one:** `ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length` (threshold 4, 3 of 3 one-minute datapoints) goes into ALARM in every intended run, because the injection pushes the queue length to about 16.0. If FIS used that alarm as its stop condition, every experiment would abort after about 3 minutes.
  - The new guardrail alarm triggers at queue length > 32 (twice the injected level) for 2 of 2 minutes. That only trips if the impact clearly goes beyond the design.
- **The existing alarm can stay as it is.** It has no AlarmActions or OKActions ("test alarm, no actions"), so these planned runs paged nobody. The ALARM state while a run is active is the expected signal.

## Execution plan

**prepare**
1. Save the current template as a rollback baseline. This is the only resource the plan changes:
   `aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 > fis-template-EXTfpFLs9urWUme-backup.json`
2. Save the alarm configuration, and confirm the guardrail alarm name isn't already taken:
   `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --region us-east-1 > alarms-backup.json`
3. Create the guardrail alarm. Check that it ends up in `OK` or `INSUFFICIENT_DATA`:
   `aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --alarm-description "FIS stop condition for EXTfpFLs9urWUme" --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0_2 --statistic Average --period 60 --evaluation-periods 2 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 --threshold 32 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching`

**pre_validate**

**apply**

**post_validate**

   `aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 --query "experimentTemplate.{stop:stopConditions,actions:actions,role:roleArn}"`
2. Check that the guardrail alarm isn't in ALARM. If it is, FIS will refuse to start the next experiment:
   `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --region us-east-1 --query "MetricAlarms[].StateValue"`

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Queue-length alarm on vol-0123456789abcdef0_2 in ALARM
**Description:** Alarm ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length (VolumeQueueLength > 4) on gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0_2 (attached to i-0123456789abcdef0_3 at /dev/sdh, us-east-1a, account 012345678901_1) was in ALARM from 01:11 to 01:15 UTC and from 15:33 to 15:47 UTC on 2026-11-11.
**Time:** 2026-11-11T15:33:08Z - 2026-11-11T15:47:08Z

### Read/write latency of about 250/503 ms on vol-0123456789abcdef0_2
**Description:** From 15:31 to 15:44 UTC on 2026-11-11, average write latency was about 503 ms (normally about 0.95 ms) and read latency about 230–261 ms (normally about 0.59 ms). Throughput fell to about 42 IOPS (0.66 MiB/s), queue length stayed at about 16, and idle time was about 0. The same pattern occurred from 01:07 to 01:12 UTC.
**Time:** 2026-11-11T15:31:00Z - 2026-11-11T15:45:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: Injected 500 ms latency capped the volume at about 42 IOPS (latency-bound, not saturated)
**Description:** With about 16 I/Os in flight at about 0.4 s each, the volume could deliver only about 42 IOPS (1.4% of the 3,000 provisioned) and about 0.66 MiB/s (0.5% of 125 MiB/s). That kept the queue length at 16, above the alarm threshold of 4. Latency set the IOPS ceiling, so the provisioned limit was never reached.
**Cascades to:** symptom-gp3-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **FIS injected 500 ms I/O latency on vol-0123456789abcdef0_2:** Experiment EXP7SDntcG3Ff1fsx (role ebs-skill-eval-fis) ran aws:ebs:volume-io-latency against vol-0123456789abcdef0_2 from 15:30:14 to 15:45:15 UTC on 2026-11-11. It added 500 ms of read latency to 50% of read I/O and 500 ms of write latency to 100% of write I/O, with no stop conditions.
- **EBS alarms in the account (all OK now):** ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length (VolumeQueueLength > 4, vol-0123456789abcdef0_2) last changed state at 15:47:08 UTC, about 2 minutes after the FIS latency action ended. That fits a return to OK. Other alarms: ebs-skill-eval-a-io2-queue-length (vol-0123456789abcdef0_18, changed 15:04), ebs-skill-eval-b-gp3-read-bytes (vol-0123456789abcdef0, changed 15:18), and the ebs-workshop alarms on vol-0123456789abcdef0_5 (changed 2026-09-18).

### Root Cause: FIS experiment EXP7SDntcG3Ff1fsx injected 500 ms EBS I/O latency
**Description:** FIS experiment EXP7SDntcG3Ff1fsx, from template EXTfpFLs9urWUme (ebs-skill-eval-d-latency, role ebs-skill-eval-fis, account 012345678901_1), ran aws:ebs:volume-io-latency against vol-0123456789abcdef0_2 from 15:30:14 to 15:45:15 UTC on 2026-11-11. It added 500 ms to 100% of writes and 50% of reads. The template has no stop conditions. An earlier 5-minute run, EXP4Xs8yABzn38YDgv (01:07–01:12 UTC), caused the 01:11–01:15 alarm. Answer to the user: do not add IOPS.
**Cascades to:** symptom-gp3-io-latency, symptom-gp3-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **FIS injected 500 ms I/O latency on vol-0123456789abcdef0_2:** Experiment EXP7SDntcG3Ff1fsx (role ebs-skill-eval-fis) ran aws:ebs:volume-io-latency against vol-0123456789abcdef0_2 from 15:30:14 to 15:45:15 UTC on 2026-11-11. It added 500 ms of read latency to 50% of read I/O and 500 ms of write latency to 100% of write I/O, with no stop conditions.
- **FIS template EXTfpFLs9urWUme targets this volume:** Template ebs-skill-eval-d-latency ("scenario d: 500 ms EBS I/O latency") targets only vol-0123456789abcdef0_2 with aws:ebs:volume-io-latency for PT15M and has no stop conditions. Both of its runs, EXP4Xs8yABzn38YDgv (01:07 UTC) and EXP7SDntcG3Ff1fsx (15:30 UTC), line up with the alarm's ALARM windows.
- **Earlier run EXP4Xs8yABzn38YDgv lines up with the 01:11 ALARM:** EXP4Xs8yABzn38YDgv used the same 500 ms latency action on vol-0123456789abcdef0_2, for PT5M, from 01:07:50 to 01:12:51 UTC. The alarm was in ALARM from 01:11 to 01:15.
- **Latency plateau matches the FIS action window to the minute:** Write latency jumped from about 0.95 ms to about 503 ms at 15:31, which is the 500 ms injected plus the baseline. It stayed flat until 15:44 and fell at 15:45, when the action ended at 15:45:15. Read latency averaged about 250 ms, consistent with 500 ms injected on 50% of reads. After injection the queued backlog drained at exactly the 3000 provisioned IOPS (about 46.9 MiB/s) until about 15:52, with queue length about 2.3. That is the workload catching up, not a separate fault.

#### Gaps
- **Who started the experiment is unconfirmed:** CloudTrail wasn't queried, so the principal that started FIS experiment EXP7SDntcG3Ff1fsx has not been confirmed.

**Description:** The user asked whether to add IOPS. During the alarm the volume used about 1.4% of its IOPS and 0.5% of its throughput.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Add a CloudWatch-alarm stop condition to FIS experiment template EXTfpFLs9urWUme; leave the volume's IOPS/throughput and the existing alarm unchanged

## Reasoning
The template has stopConditions source=none, so nothing halts an injection that goes beyond its design. The existing alarm (threshold 4) fires on every intended run (queue ~16), so a separate guardrail alarm at queue length > 32 for 2 of 2 minutes is used. The existing alarm has no actions, so planned runs page nobody. Plan passed the safe-deployment policy check; not executed.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Save the template as a rollback baseline
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 > fis-template-EXTfpFLs9urWUme-backup.json
```
**Purpose:** Save the template as a rollback baseline
**Advisory:** Confirm the backup matches template ID EXTfpFLs9urWUme before continuing

#### 1.2 Save alarm config and confirm the guardrail name is free
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --region us-east-1 > alarms-backup.json
```
**Purpose:** Save alarm config and confirm the guardrail name is free

#### 1.3 Create the guardrail alarm; confirm it is OK or INSUFFICIENT_DATA
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --alarm-description "FIS stop condition for EXTfpFLs9urWUme" --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0_2 --statistic Average --period 60 --evaluation-periods 2 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 --threshold 32 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching
```
**Purpose:** Create the guardrail alarm; confirm it is OK or INSUFFICIENT_DATA

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Stop here if any run is pending, initiating or running
**Type:** command
```
aws fis list-experiments --experiment-template-id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 --query "experiments[].{id:id,status:state.status}"
```
**Purpose:** Stop here if any run is pending, initiating or running

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Add the guardrail alarm as the template's stop condition
**Type:** command
```
aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 --stop-conditions source=aws:cloudwatch:alarm,value=[redacted ARN]
```
**Purpose:** Add the guardrail alarm as the template's stop condition
**Advisory:** Role ebs-skill-eval-fis needs cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms; if missing, the next experiment fails to start (safe failure). Not checked.

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm the stop condition is set and actions, targets and role are…
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 --query "experimentTemplate.{stop:stopConditions,actions:actions,role:roleArn}"
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the stop condition is set and actions, targets and role are unchanged

#### 4.2 Confirm the guardrail is not in ALARM (FIS would refuse to start)
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --region us-east-1 --query "MetricAlarms[].StateValue"
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the guardrail is not in ALARM (FIS would refuse to start)

#### 4.3 Prove the guardrail does not abort intended runs
**Type:** text
Optionally run the template once in a planned window: it should complete the full 15 minutes with the guardrail staying out of ALARM.
**Purpose:** Prove the guardrail does not abort intended runs

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Put back the original stop conditions
**Type:** command
```
aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 --stop-conditions source=none
```
**Purpose:** Put back the original stop conditions

#### 5.2 Delete the guardrail alarm once no longer referenced
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch delete-alarms --alarm-names ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Delete the guardrail alarm once no longer referenced

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Make stop conditions mandatory for every FIS template
**Description:** Define the guardrail alarm and aws:cloudwatch:alarm stop condition in IaC wherever ebs-skill-eval resources (Project=ebs-skill-eval, Name=ebs-skill-eval-d-latency) are defined, so redeploys don't reintroduce source: none.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The template deployed from code has a non-none stop condition
- Creating a template with source: none is blocked by review or policy check

#### 2. Document alarm behavior during experiments
**Description:** Record in the alarm description or runbook that ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length enters ALARM during every planned run of EXTfpFLs9urWUme and is not a reason to add IOPS.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Responders can match the alarm to a planned FIS run without investigating

#### 3. Avoid paging during experiments if actions are added later

{"id": "2935b7b6-9f3b-4c6b-97d3-91dd43c37dae", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_wGMbeU3vr3fw22CVLSqqzq", "content": [{"text": "     1	---
     2	name: storage-ebs-expertise
     3	description: >
     4	  Use this skill when a user wants to know why Amazon EBS storage is slow, why an
     5	  EBS alarm fired, or whether their EBS setup is production-ready, even if they only

     9	  VolumeAvgReadLatency, BurstBalance) or EBSIOBalance%/EBSByteBalance%; for sizing
     10	  IOPS or throughput changes; for a volume modification that looks stuck or failed;
     11	  for deciding which snapshots or AMIs are safe to delete or how to recover them;
     12	  for KMS errors on encrypted volumes; for EBS quota or limit errors; for a jump in
     13	  the EBS bill; and for a pre-launch EBS review. Do not use it for S3, EFS, FSx,
     14	  instance store, or EC2 problems unrelated to EBS.
     15	metadata:
     16	  author: dewavic
     17	  version: "1.0.0"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS KMS, AWS CloudTrail, Service Quotas"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     21	---
     22	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     23	
     24	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     25	
     26	## When to Use This Skill
     27	
     28	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     29	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     30	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     31	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots are safe to delete.
     32	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     33	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     34	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     35	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     36	
     37	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     38	
     39	## Prerequisites
     40	
     41	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     42	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     43	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     44	
     45	---
     46	
     47	## Workflow
     48	
     49	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     50	
     51	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     52	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     53	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     54	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     55	
     56	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     57	
     58	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     59	|---|---|---|
     60	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     61	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     62	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     63	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     64	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     65	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     66	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     67	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     68	
     69	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     70	
     71	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     72	
     73	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     74	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     75	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     76	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     77	
     78	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     79	
     80	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     81	
     82	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     83	
     84	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     85	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     86	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, or Not applicable.
     87	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     88	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     89	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     90	
     91	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every review answer starts with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`.
     92	
     93	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     94	
     95	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     96	
     97	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     98	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom.
     99	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     100	- Every "safe to delete" verdict is backed by the checks its tier requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not safe to delete.
     101	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     102	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     103	
     104	---
     105	
     106	## Critical Rules
     107	
     108	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, DeleteSnapshot, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     109	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     110	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     111	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     112	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     113	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     114	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     115	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. AWS CloudTrail is optional; `DescribeVolumesModifications` is the change record.
     116	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     117	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     118	
     119	## Error Handling
     120	
     121	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.

{"id": "cae41471-33eb-4fa4-bb14-74d64288611b", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "**The answer to "Should we add more IOPS?" is no.** The alarm on `vol-0123456789abcdef0_2` fired because a planned AWS FIS experiment deliberately added 500 ms of latency to the volume's I/O. The volume never ran out of capacity: during the run it handled about 42 IOPS, which is 1.4% of the 3,000 provisioned. Adding IOPS would have changed nothing. The incident has already recovered on its own. The weak spot still open is that the experiment template has no stop condition, so the plan below adds one.

I proposed this plan but did not run it. It passed the safe-deployment policy check with no violations.

## Mitigation summary

**Action:** Add a CloudWatch-alarm stop condition to FIS experiment template `EXTfpFLs9urWUme`. Don't change the volume's IOPS or throughput, and keep the existing alarm as it is.

**Reasoning:**
- **What I read today (account `012345678901_1`, us-east-1):**
  - The template still has `stopConditions: [{"source": "none"}]`. It runs `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` against `[redacted ARN]` for PT15M, using role `ebs-skill-eval-fis`.
  - Both runs from this template (`EXP7SDntcG3Ff1fsx` and `EXP4Xs8yABzn38YDgv`) are `completed`.
  - The volume is unchanged: gp3, 20 GiB, 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, `in-use` on `i-0123456789abcdef0_3` as `/dev/sdh`.
- **Why a stop condition:** right now nothing stops an injection if it hurts more than intended. A run could take longer, be pointed at the wrong volume, or hit a production workload, and it would still run its full 15 minutes.
- **Why a separate guardrail alarm, not the existing one:** `ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length` (threshold 4, 3 of 3 one-minute datapoints) goes into ALARM in every intended run, because the injection pushes the queue length to about 16.0. If FIS used that alarm as its stop condition, every experiment would abort after about 3 minutes.
  - The new guardrail alarm triggers at queue length > 32 (twice the injected level) for 2 of 2 minutes. That only trips if the impact clearly goes beyond the design.
- **The existing alarm can stay as it is.** It has no AlarmActions or OKActions ("test alarm, no actions"), so these planned runs paged nobody. The ALARM state while a run is active is the expected signal.

## Execution plan

**prepare**
1. Save the current template as a rollback baseline. This is the only resource the plan changes:
   `aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 > fis-template-EXTfpFLs9urWUme-backup.json`
2. Save the alarm configuration, and confirm the guardrail alarm name isn't already taken:
   `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --region us-east-1 > alarms-backup.json`
3. Create the guardrail alarm. Check that it ends up in `OK` or `INSUFFICIENT_DATA`:
   `aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --region us-east-1 --alarm-name ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --alarm-description "FIS stop condition for EXTfpFLs9urWUme" --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0_2 --statistic Average --period 60 --evaluation-periods 2 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 --threshold 32 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching`
   - Advisory: make sure the saved baseline matches the template ID above before you go on.

**pre_validate**
1. Confirm no experiment from this template is pending, initiating or running. If one is, stop here:
   `aws fis list-experiments --experiment-template-id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 --query "experiments[].{id:id,status:state.status}"`

**apply**
1. Attach the stop condition. Only `stopConditions` changes; actions, targets and role stay the same:
   `aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 --stop-conditions source=aws:cloudwatch:alarm,value=[redacted ARN]`
   - Advisory: role `ebs-skill-eval-fis` needs `cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms` for the stop condition to be checked. If it's missing, the next experiment fails to start, which is a safe failure. I did not check the role's policy.

**post_validate**
1. Check that the template now lists the guardrail alarm ARN as its stop condition, and that actions, targets and role match the backup:
   `aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 --query "experimentTemplate.{stop:stopConditions,actions:actions,role:roleArn}"`
2. Check that the guardrail alarm isn't in ALARM. If it is, FIS will refuse to start the next experiment:
   `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --region us-east-1 --query "MetricAlarms[].StateValue"`
3. Optionally, run the template once in a planned window. The test passes if the run completes its full 15 minutes and the guardrail alarm stays out of ALARM.

**rollback**
1. Put back the original stop conditions:
   `aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXTfpFLs9urWUme --region us-east-1 --stop-conditions source=none`
2. Only after the template no longer references it, delete the guardrail alarm:
   `aws cloudwatch delete-alarms --alarm-names ebs-skill-eval-d-fis-guardrail --region us-east-1`

## Code change spec (permanent prevention)

No repository URL was available. Apply these changes wherever the `ebs-skill-eval` resources are defined (the tags are `Project=ebs-skill-eval`, `Name=ebs-skill-eval-d-latency`).

1. **Make stop conditions mandatory for every FIS template.**
   - **Change:** define the guardrail alarm and the `aws:cloudwatch:alarm` stop condition in infrastructure as code, so that redeploying the template doesn't bring back `source: none`.
   - **Done when:**
     - The template deployed from code has a non-`none` stop condition.
     - Creating a template with `source: none` is blocked by review or a policy check.
2. **Document how the alarm behaves during experiments.**
   - **Change:** record in the alarm description or runbook that `ebs-skill-eval-d-gp3-queue-length` goes into ALARM during every planned run of `EXTfpFLs9urWUme`, and that this alarm is not a reason to add IOPS.
   - **Done when:** whoever responds to the alarm can match it to a planned FIS run without investigating.
3. **Keep the existing alarm from paging during experiments (only if you later add actions).**
   - **Change:** if AlarmActions are ever added, wrap the alarm in a composite alarm that ignores it while an experiment is running.
   - **Done when:** a planned experiment pages nobody.

## Separate findings and gaps

- **The 15:46–15:51 UTC load period (not confirmed).** The volume ran flat at about 3,000 IOPS, its provisioned limit, at 0.95 ms latency. This has nothing to do with the alarm, and on its own it doesn't justify adding IOPS.
  - Before resizing, check the volume over a representative period (for example 7 days of 1-minute p99 IOPS and latency).
  - The instance's EBS baseline of 6,000 IOPS / 149.0 MiB/s leaves headroom if the volume ever does need to be resized.
- **Gaps:**
  - I didn't read the IAM policy on `ebs-skill-eval-fis`.
  - I didn't look for a pipeline, because this is a manually managed FIS template.
